items.title: Amazon’s Trainium Takes a Strike at the Training King
items.content:
Trainium has already proven itself in the realm of inference. Anthropic is running production inference and RL rollouts on Trainium2 and Trainium3. Historically, Trainium has been great for inference but not the best fit for research training. In inference, the model architecture changes at a much slower pace compared to training, where researchers iterate on many different experiments and ablations of model architecture and need a stack that covers a broad API surface. In the past, that is where Trainium fell short.
 The AWS Neuron team is aggressively working to change this pitfall with the biggest shift being moving towards a first-class, native PyTorch training experience. Gone are the days of sprinkling xm.step() through your training loop and wrestling with a bespoke XLA-style execution model. Trainium now runs PyTorch the way PyTorch users expect, in eager mode, with torch.compile and the standard APIs.
 The SemiAnalysis engineering team has been trying out the Trainium3 racks for the past couple of weeks and has found the experience to be great – we love the overall direction of where it is heading. To be clear, it isn’t perfect yet, and we have personally run into a couple of bugs ourselves. It’s nowhere close to the maturity of the CUDA ecosystem, but the direction is right. Their team is making rapid progress with the help of agentic coding.
 Furthermore, unlike other accelerator companies, where we had to fight tooth and nail to get their engineers a reasonably stable CI fleet, Trainium uses up to 80,000 physical cores allocated towards automated quality control.
 In this article, we walk through our experience on the Trainium3 TorchTitan and TorchNeuron stack, along with our experience of Trainium’s Neuron Explorer profiler, which is way better than both Nvidia’s and AMD’s profilers. We created a bunch of demos to show how Trainium’s profiler is “GPU Impossible.” 

 Visualizing Nafea Bshara, VP at AWS In Trainium Profiler Showcasing Trainium’s Finegrain Profiler. Source: SemiAnalysis 
 In an upcoming article, we will go deep on writing speed-of-light NKI kernels and microbenchmarking on Trainium3. For our deep dive into the Trainium hardware, check out our previous article where we do a complete hardware breakdown.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 We Are Hiring SemiAnalysis is hiring for various Member of Technical Staff roles. If you find this type of analysis interesting, apply below:
 Apply Here 
 What we’re looking for:
 Highly motivated & skilled Member of Technical Staff to join our growing engineering team. 
 Member of Technical Staff will play a crucial role in developing inference benchmarks & system modeling 
 You will also play a role in writing and preparing our newsletter articles for publishing, with the opportunity for direct authorship recognition. 
 We are hiring individual contributors at all experience levels. Compensation will be competitive 
 As part of the interview process, you’ll complete a paid coding challenge designed to reflect typical daily tasks at SemiAnalysis 
 Competitive Compensation depending on experience, skillset, location & business needs 
 Qualifications 
 Proactive, self-motivated, and capable of working independently in a global team. 
 Demonstrated experience in ML frameworks such as PyTorch or JAX through professional experience, personal projects, or personal Substack blogs 
 Solid understanding of at least 1 of the following: transformer architecture, LLM parallelism strategies, and/or CUDA parallel programming 
 Strong research skills and the ability to synthesize information from various sources to draw insights. 
 English language proficiency required, Chinese language proficiency preferred 
 Moving Towards a First-Class PyTorch Experience Amazon has made a major course correction to its software strategy, and we believe it will meaningfully broaden Trainium3 adoption. TorchNeuron represents a native PyTorch experience instead of duct-taping Trainium onto PyTorch through the PyTorch/XLA project. The new backend is aimed at everyone who isn’t a frontier-lab kernel engineer. AWS has even hired the lead of Google’s native Torch on TPU effort to work on native Torch for Trainium. He was the TPU SW lead from the start of the program at Google, including XLA, xprof, Cloud TPU, etc.
 The old approach made Trainium feel foreign to anyone coming from CUDA. PyTorch/XLA relied on lazy tensor graph capture and had no first-class eager mode. It also didn’t support PyTorch’s native distributed APIs (torch.distributed.*) or its native parallelism APIs (DTensor, SimpleFSDP, DDP). Users had to rely on out-of-tree XLA SPMD APIs such as torch_xla.experimental.spmd_fsdp and torch_xla.distributed.spmd. For researchers who are used to native PyTorch on CUDA, switching to Trainium meant relearning how to write a training loop.

 Source: AWS 
 The pain of converting GPU research codebases by adding XLA markers everywhere was a massive turnoff to anyone who used PyTorch/XLA before.

 Source: AWS 
 At a high level, the only change needed is replacing .to(”cuda”) with .to(”neuron”), and in theory the vast majority of the PyTorch ATen operators will work decently well out of the box.

 Source: AWS 
 In theory, with PyTorch’s torch.accelerator hardware-agnostic API, lines of code like bf16 autocast won’t even need to be changed, though some APIs in PyTorch and some research codebases still haven’t migrated to the torch.accelerator namespace and still directly call the torch.cuda.* namespace.
 As most academics and researchers across robotics, biotech, world models, and self-driving mainly use BF16, Trainium Torch will not support TorchAO MXFP8 on day 0 until they have made the BF16 training experience great. We don’t disagree with this sequence, as most people doing MXFP8 training are big Tier 1 labs that have enough kernel engineers to write custom kernels for the big training run.
 Trainium Torch Ecosystem PyTorch is popular not only because of core PyTorch but also because of the entire ecosystem of libraries, including Hugging Face Transformers, PEFT, diffusers, TRL, Accelerate, TorchTitan, etc. We are amazed to see that Trainium Torch already supports a ton of these libraries in the ecosystem, including Hugging Face Accelerate, which an insane number of layers of indirection. Trainium supports one of the most popular clean open-source training codebases called TorchTitan with many Tier 2 labs forking it to serve as the foundation of their internal training codebase. Trainium’s new PyTorch experience fully supports that too.
 We saw how Google was able to successfully partner with Inferact/RadixArk to bring TPUs into the vLLM/SGLang ecosystem, and also land Meta as a production TPU customer. Furthermore, by bringing TPUs into the vLLM/SGLang ecosystem, TPUs were already able to automatically get day 0 support for Muse Spark Open and commitments for day 0 TPU support for popular upcoming models.
 While it is true that the increase in agentic coding has made the engine code itself less important, what vLLM/SGLang brings to the table is the ecosystem. No matter the open source model, on day 0, the global ML community trusts vLLM/SGLang as the go-to engine for inference. No vibe-coded engine has that reach.
 We are starting to see Trainium rapidly invest in the vLLM/SGLang community with hardware access and early access to Trainium on SGLang built on native PyTorch (TorchNeuron), similar to the TorchTPU approach. 

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 TorchTitan Experience TorchTitan is one of the most popular open-source pre-training frameworks, and we tested Neuron’s support to gauge the user experience of a researcher training a non-trivial model with Trainium. Specifically, we trained a Qwen3-32B on 16 Trainium2 chips, 64 LNC=2 logical cores in total, and we also tried doing it on a rack-scale Trainium3 UltraServer with 64 physical chips.
 Overall, we liked the user experience, though there were some rough edges that the Amazon team already has on its roadmap to fix.
 While we will provide the Trainium2 MFU below for completeness, the part to focus on is that for ML research ablations, what matters most isn’t a speed-of-light-optimized stack but decent performance and broad support across model architecture modifications, so researchers can iterate without fighting the stack.
 With Neuron’s official TorchTitan image, we were able to launch the run without any issues. We measured 11,099 tokens per second in average training throughput on eager mode, at 23.89% MFU . For compiled mode, we saw 14,156 tokens per second and 30.47% MFU, a 1.28x throughput improvement over eager mode. We tried changing the model architecture slightly in the modeling code and it worked great also.
 Neuron also offers training recipes for more modern model architectures, so we tested its gpt-oss 20B training recipe. Neuron supports gpt-oss training through integration with GraphTrainer , TorchTitan’s experimental trainer module. Specifically, Neuron adds Trainium-compatible configurations of SimpleFSDP, a compilation backend for PyTorch computation graph capture, and custom NKI kernels for attention and MoE operations. In terms of user experience, the recipe worked out of the box, and everything went well.
 One thing that was not yet implemented using the upstream APIs was TokenSwitch. In the age of MoE, for inference and training, MoE combine and MoE dispatch are among the most important comms ops and take anywhere from 60-70% of the communication volume, and TokenSwitch is PyTorch’s first-class API for them. Trainium doesn’t support it yet and instead relies on a custom TorchTitan class called NeuronEPTokenDispatcher. Moving it onto the TokenSwitch API looks like a simple fix, and the AWS team has committed to collaborating with the Meta PyTorch team to modify the TokenSwitch ABC such that it can support Trainium too.
 The part where it was slightly disappointing was the Neuron compiler took a long time to compile, leading to a long wait in the first step. Concretely, the first step took 184.6 seconds for eager mode (255.7 seconds for compiled mode), which is 30-55x longer than the average step time, excluding the first step. For gpt-oss, this training run came at a ridiculously high compilation time of 27 minutes and 17 seconds, which leads to a terrible user experience, especially for researchers who experiment with new model architectures. The reason for this is that historically the Trainium compiler stack has mainly been focused on inference, where compile time doesn’t matter because compilation is done offline and cached once per image and doesn’t affect production inference, whereas in training it does. While this is the right call for inference at the time, for researchers iterating on model architecture, that’s a meaningful friction point.
 The Neuron team is already addressing this directly. Upcoming TorchNeuron releases introduce a new compiler backend with a broad set of precompiled NKI kernels and a compile stack re-architected for fast compilation, targeting up to a 2 orders of magnitude reduction in time-to-first-step for both eager and compiled modes, with minimal or no performance regression. If they deliver on that, compilation time stops being a conversation.
 Training MatMul Performance One of the most important things for experimental training is to have decent performance across a broad range of shapes as ML researchers try lots of different things. We benchmarked a single Trainium3 logical core (LNC=2) on the PyTorch nn.functional.linear API to understand its matrix multiplication performance, and we compared it with GB300 and B200 for reference. We swept through the matrix shapes of projection operations in major open weight models, and we set the M dimension to 1, 128, and 2048 to represent different batch size scenarios.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 In our benchmark, Trainium3 achieved a visibly higher MFU than GB300, starting from the mid-range, where the matrix multiplication performs 1 GFLOP of computation. It was only after 100 GFLOP that GB300 and B200 started outperforming Trainium3, and Trainium3 won again after 1 TFLOP.
 FlexAttention API FlexAttention is a high-level API that allows implementing different attention variants using PyTorch, while offering backward pass auto-generation and reasonable performance. Good FlexAttention support shows a hardware’s flexibility and ease-of-use to researchers. We ran the FlexAttention benchmark suite on Trainium3 to see its FlexAttention support.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 Overall, Trainium3 passed 89 out of 96 test cases, a 93% pass rate. All 7 failed cases were at large batch size (4) and sequence length (8192), and all failed due to compilation exceeding the time budget rather than numerical errors . These issues will be fixed in later versions of TorchNeuron.
 Additionally, we tried implementing custom attention variants not in the FlexAttention benchmark suite for Trainium3, and it matched the numerics of Nvidia GPUs.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 Automated Quality Assurance SemiAnalysis is known in the global ML community to be the “CI Karen,” setting a high bar across all hardware vendors and doing whatever it takes to get senior leadership of AI chip companies to actually provide their engineers with enough resources and CI fleet to maintain a high bar of automated quality control.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 One recent achievement, which took over 9 months of fighting with AMD senior leadership, was getting their engineers enough stable nodes to achieve 93% parity on gating test groups. 

 Source: vLLM Dashboard 
 Inference is a narrow problem. A lab serving a handful of production models needs a forward pass, mostly fixed architectures, and a small set of hot kernels.
 Training is a generality problem. Each of the thousands of operators needs a backward pass, and research codebases sometimes accidentally run operators in higher precision, which must also be supported. To ensure that Trainium works across a wide range of model architectures and can do eager mode and compile mode well, AWS collected a giant list of top 100k+ Hugging Face models that spread across a whole range of different normalization, MLP, MoE layouts and attention types. Not only do they test that it doesn’t crash, but they also test performance, which ops use CPU fallbacks and don’t have native support yet, where graph breaks are and most importantly, they test numerics against CPU and Nvidia baselines. They test tensor level parity and loss curve divergence also. It is easy to finish an exam within 10 minutes, but it doesn’t matter how fast you finish an exam if you get a 0% on it. Same thing with training stacks. It is easy to get decent MFU%, but it is hard to get decent MFU% while not introducing numeric issues.

 Source: AWS 
 Although the pass rates aren’t at 100% yet, what matters is the trajectory. AWS is climbing rapidly, with agent swarms systematically fixing the remaining failures. We think it’s a strength that AWS’s internal summary table, the one senior leadership sees, shows gaps transparently rather than hiding them.
 We say this from experience. When SemiAnalysis and upstream maintainers have tried to fix quality control culture at other hardware vendors, we’ve found that senior leadership is genuinely shocked when shown the real parity pass rates. At one vendor in particular, there was so much middle management filtering that by the time CI numbers reached senior leadership, they showed 99.99%, while the actual gating parity pass rate at the time was below 5%.
 Neuron Explorer - Better than Nvidia and AMD Profilers Trainium’s profiler is by far leading the industry and is SOTA status. Here we share our initial impressions and plan on sharing our full user experience in a future Trainium kernel article.
 Trainium’s profiler is loved by all the performance engineers at Anthropic. Anthropic’s head of performance (who is ex-Jane and Finch Street) has publicly said that performance analysis on Trainium is way better than performance analysis on Nvidia GPUs (and obviously better than on AMD GPUs).

 Source: Tristan Hume on Twitter 
 We agree with Tristan Hume. In our experience, the profiling experience was amazing, after getting over the initial hump of the profiling setup being slightly confusing (but not impossible). There are multiple environment variables to set, different file types to save, and various commands to capture and view the profile traces. This is only the kernel profiling setup, and the PyTorch profiling setup is similar but with slight differences, making things even more confusing. With the help of Codex ( since since during the beginning time of testing Trainium, Claude refuses to write Trainium kernels , but that has since been fixed by Anthropic), our best effort working setup is as follows:
 Launch a persistent Neuron Explorer server
 Profile the kernel with neuron-explorer capture command
 Upload the profile trace as an artifact to the Neuron Explorer server as a web request
 We shared feedback with AWS that we wished the documentation could be clearer on the workflow, explaining what environment variables need to be set for what reasons, and what purpose each file type serves.
 Once the setup is done, the profiler user experience is great. Neuron Explorer is co-designed with the hardware. We particularly like the timeline separating hardware units in different rows, so that bubbles are visible at a glance. In contrast, GPU programmers have to roll their own setup for intra-SM profiling as the official Nsight tools don’t support that.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 We also like how the viewer visualizes dependencies. When a block is selected, its dependencies and dependents light up in different colors, which helps us reason about work overlapping, e.g. whether computation sufficiently overlaps with memory loading. The image below shows that the selected white block is:
 Flow-dependent on the red block
 Order-dependent on the orange block
 A flow dependency of the blue block
 An output dependency of the purple block

 Neuron Explorer dependency visualization. Source: SemiAnalysis 

 Neuron Explorer code editor mapping. Source: SemiAnalysis 

 Neuron Explorer: Event information when hovering on an event. Source: SemiAnalysis 

 Neuron Explorer memory bank utilization visualization. Source: SemiAnalysis 

 Neuron Explorer microsecond-level memory throughput visualization. Source: SemiAnalysis 
 Trainium Profiler Demo - Pixel Art Neuron Explorer has many more features, including code editor mapping, MFU estimation, memory usage, and even creating pixel art due to how precise the profiler is. The images below are all from profiler traces of running on actual Trainium hardware, not fake profile reports. We were mainly inspired by the Bad Apple post from Daniel Liu (Anthropic Performance Engineer) and have created our own agentic coding SKILL.md for creating images. We did not have the time yet to create one to automatically generate videos frame by frame but will in the future and open source this SKILL.md for everyone to use. We mainly generate this pixel art by using the 16 DMA engines per physical core by “coloring in” regions by turning the DMA engines active, and the width of the shaded area is determined by how much data we have each DMA engine move.

 Bad Apple on Neuron Explorer. Source: Daniel Liu 

 Visualizing the SemiAnalysis logo. Source: SemiAnalysis 

 Visualizing Jeff Bezos (pre looksmaxxing). Source: SemiAnalysis 

 Visualizing Dylan Patel (pre looksmaxxing). Source: SemiAnalysis 
 Since AWS is a partner of Nvidia, Jensen should tell his engineers to book a meeting with the AWS Trainium team on the hardware features needed to do accurate fine-grained profiling such that Nvidia can learn how to add this capability to Feynman or Feynman-Next GPUs.

 Visualizing Jensen on Trainium3. Source: SemiAnalysis 
 Nvidia’s intra-kernel profiler Nsight

items.title: The Huawei-DeepSeek Symbiosis
items.content:
Right before China’s national day holidays, DeepSeek released Ascend support for TileLang , DeepGEMM , DeepEP , TileKernels , FlashMLA , and DeepSelect .
 Neither can do this alone. Although they have Pangu, Huawei has no frontier lab to prove their chip can train or infer models, DeepSeek has models but cannot buy the compute it needs. Each supplies exactly what the other lacks: Huawei provides the hardware and native software stack; DeepSeek brings the workloads and engineering needed to make that hardware useful for its models. September 30’s release of Ascend support in DeepSeek repositories is an artifact of this trade, where the exchange runs through the kernel-authoring language.

 Source: SemiAnalysis - Note that the diagram is a simulation. 
 In 2028 or even 2027, DeepSeek will likely be primarily using Huawei’s stack, especially with the external and internal pressure to build a fully domestic chinese ecosystem. As we show here and in future articles, the Huawei ecosystem is already mature and well developed, with strong foundations from the Ascend time and DeepSeek engineers building further ontop.
 In this article, we’ll first examine Ascend 950PR’s architecture and benchmark its compute and memory performance. We then explore DeepSeek’s software releases, from TileLang’s compiler capabilities to hardware-specific kernel optimizations and rack-scale communication. Finally, we analyze DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash’s execution profile.
 Ascend 950 We deep-dived into CANN and the Ascend 950 architecture in our DeepSeek V4 Pro article . Since then, more interesting details have been revealed.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 Starting from the chip, many variants of 950PR/DT have appeared with varying core counts, HBM stack height, and cache sizes. Some are likely either virtualised/simulated, or for testing only. This is because only a fraction of dies and HBM stacks meet the target spec, due to both outright defects and parametric shortfalls in power and performance, so Huawei bins both compute and memory into multiple SKUs and pairs weaker memory with weaker compute, rather than binning only compute as Nvidia does.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 This isn’t new, 910B also has variants such as 910B1, 910B2, 910B3, 910B4. For the following microbenchmarks, we use an Ascend 950PR_9579, with 28 cube cores and 128 GiB HBM.
 root@cb3bb851f93f:/workspace# npu-smi info

| 0 | Ascend950PR | OK | 203.3 56 0 / 0 |

 Running point chases reading 16 KiB of integer payload per launch, it stays near 134ns through 18 blocks, rises to 182ns at 56, then jumps to 391ns at 64. This is consistent with a second wave beyond 56 Vector cores.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 Then by running a scalar pointer-chase probe separately on every Cube and Vector core, recording load timings at matching addresses throughout a 128 MiB chain, we get the following graph. Each cell’s color represents the mean absolute difference between two cores' address profiles, producing two groups that match the decoded dies.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 Going further, by timing a Vector core’s pointer chase while another core runs either memory traffic or register-only work; the extra slowdown reveals which subsystems share resources, supporting groups such as {0,2,4} and {1,3,5}. Mixed Cube/Vector launches identify each subsystem’s one Cube and two Vectors, which we draw together within those groups, with physical positions remaining schematic.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 CPU within the NPU Each 950PR comes with a variable number of Linx816 AArch64 ELF AICPUs. The MIDR numbers imply these cores are likely the same as the middle cores in the Kirin 9000S/9010. These AICPU cores have instruction set:
 fp asimd evtstrm aes pmull sha1 sha2 crc32 atomics fphp asimdhp cpuid
asimdrdm jscvt fcma lrcpc dcpop sha3 sm3 sm4 asimddp sha512 sve
asimdfhm dit uscat ilrcpc flagm ssbs sb paca pacg dcpodp flagm2
frint svei8mm svebf16 i8mm bf16 dgh rng ecv 
 For this SKU, there are 7 configured, 6 visible, and 5 executing AICPU cores. Other than device control it can provide CPU-operator support, such as KV metadata. The AICPU helps out for short work where D2H overhead take up most of the time.
 For DSA, a small scheduling step reads the current sequence lengths and assigns indexer work to accelerator cores. Cube/Vector cores then compute INT8 indexer scores and select the top 2,048 indices. These planning, index selection, and gather steps are ran on AICPUs in vLLM-ascend implementation, and we compare their performance to running on the host CPU.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 Due to their limited compute performance, AICPU is only good for short work where overhead dominates, and work where data starts and is consumed at the NPU.
 Microbenchmarks Ascend 950PR is designed for prefill and recommendation. It gets lower memory bandwidth and core than its bigger brother the 950DT.
 The results below are not from DeepSeek’s contributions but from stock torch.matmul on ascend resolving to aclnnMatmul_MatMulV3Common_MatMulV3 . We compared 1,055 BF16 GEMM shapes from several open-sourced models. Huawei’s best kernels hits 99.7% of the ceiling, showing DeepSeek’s 99+% from DeepGEMM isn’t the only way to maximize utilization. Huawei engineers did good work too.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 The advantage is concentrated in compute-bound work. On the shapes below Ascend’s ridge, its median achieved/attainable fraction is 41.5% versus H100’s 46.8%. Some of Nvidia’s results were power-limited and did not hit maximum SM clock: median power around 690-698 W out of a 700 W limit, and median sampled SM clocks at 1335-1470 MHz, below the max of 1830 MHz. Huawei approximated 599-600 W, at 1500-1550 MHz against its 1650 MHz reference.
 Ascend’s MXU design may contribute to some of this high utilization, Ascend stages matrix operands in dedicated L0A/L0B buffers and accumulators in L0C, with overlapping movement, computation and result handling. Huawei associates the enlarged L0C with more flexible tiling and reuse.
 But of course, 950PR’s falls behind on absolute values, sitting somewhere between A100 and MI300X.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 MemBW Measuring HBM memory bandwidth, we see 950PR’s effective bandwidth and bandwidth utilization surpassing H100 at small message size per buffers, and nearly matching H100 in bandwidth utilization at large message sizes.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 A dip appears in the curve as Ascend switches copy methods to a Vector-core TensorMove kernel that has more startup cost, so a slightly larger copy suddenly takes longer. For very large copies, that extra cost becomes relatively small, so bandwidth rises again.
 Note that high FLOPs utilization and bandwidth utilization does not necessarily translate to high MFU/MBU. Training, especially with FSDP, requires collectives, checkpointing, and data moving that can be hard to overlap. 
 As we mentioned in our Jalepeno article, a “chip” in benchmarks is just a social construct. Multiple dies can be glue to form a bigger “chip”. Thus performance per watt or TCO is the best comparison. But for China, watts are far cheaper. We’ll analyze Ascend’s perf per TCO in a future article.

 Hardware raises the ceiling, but software lets you reach that ceiling. Although Huawei’s hardware may be beyond ~5 years behind(compared to A100), the software is right at the frontier.
 DeepSeek Open Source For the 6 repos that received ascend support( TileLang , DeepGEMM , DeepEP , TileKernels , FlashMLA , DeepSelect ), only TileLang is usable as of writing, and CANN 9.2.0 has not been released. Deepseek requires CANN 9.2.0 which was released after time of writing, and a C++20 compiler is required which CANN 9.2.0-beta.2 does not provide. The HDK will be released on Oct 15 . This comes after DeepSeek’s open source week in 2025, where some of these repositories were released with Nvidia support only.
 From the results above, we can see Huawei can already execute operations well; the symbiosis is about making the rest of the application & the work required to support it more efficient and reusable.
 Engineering runs both ways Huawei’s architecture is already influencing how DeepSeek’s software organizes data. Earlier FlashMLA KV-cache layouts stored quantized values and their scaling factors in separate regions. On Ascend, fetching a token then required separate transfers for its values and scales. The new implementation places them together, reducing the number of transfer requests by the memory transfer engine(MTE).

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 From fast kernels to reusable kernel engineering Ascend 950 backend is merged into the main TileLang repository, rather than existing only in a separate Huawei adapter. It adds native compilation, scheduling, synchronization and runtime integration for Ascend’s execution model.
 TileLang makes Ascend kernels easier to write, but developers still need to account for the hardware. They choose the calculations, tile sizes and where data is stored. The compiler handles much of the coordination between Cube cores, Vector cores and data transfers.
 Digging below the implementation and looking at its performance against CANN and Triton-ascend, it can match and beat CANN at certain cases; the preferred implementation changes with size. This is a warm-cache simple and naive benchmark.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 AutoSchedule uses data dependencies and estimated execution times to plan which operations can overlap. It also chooses how many buffer slots to use within the available on-chip memory, allowing upcoming data to load while the current tile is being processed. Developers can guide these decisions when the default schedule is not suitable.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 On 950PR, AutoSchedule helps especially for smaller sizes, reducing execution time by up to 40% for a single operation.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 The compiler also inserts synchronization so operations wait for the data they need, while removing waits that other dependencies make unnecessary. It checks conditional branches too, so it does not assume an operation has completed when that branch might never execute. This reduces the synchronization work programmers must manage themselves.
 DeepEP Huawei has joined NVIDIA in commercializing large scale-up AI systems, with its Ascend supernodes extending tightly coupled accelerator interconnects across multiple racks from the 910 CloudMatrix384 to the 950 SuperPod,enabling wideEP scale-out. In the 30th September release, Huawei also released EP16 dispatch/combine benchmarks over URMA in the 950DT superpod.

 Source: Huawei , DeepSeek , SemiAnalysis 
 Huawei’s dispatch is three sequential operators (pre/URMA/post) whereas GB300 is one fused call, and their post work includes receive completion, which our measurement includes, but also includes expansion by expert which GB300’s results don’t.
 DeepEP-Ascend is a port of DeepEP V2.5, with the same python API but calls URMA and HCCL underneath. In July 2025, Huawei’s Ascend team proposed DeepEP-Ascend under deepseek-ai , but a DeepEP maintainer declined . Today, DeepEP-Ascend is distributed under DeepSeek’s own organization.
 Ascend’s separate Cube and Vector execution paths create opportunities to overlap communication and computation, but do not make that overlap free. Expert computation can also require vector processing and data movement, while communication competes for shared memory bandwidth. Therefore there’s a tradeoff on how much communication can be hidden without slowing the computation that runs alongside.

 Source: Huawei 
 This resource-balancing problem is not unique to DeepSeek. Huawei’s Kimi K3 recipe explicitly restricts vector use to leave capacity for concurrent work, and chooses between dedicated CCU and Vector-based communication according to what must overlap. Faster individual operations are not enough: their resource demands must also fit together.
 DeepEP-Ascend’s documentation identifies contention between combine processing and URMA communication for HBM resources, and says Huawei firmware improvements are planned to reduce it. This is the practical form of co-design: the model exposes a bottleneck, the implementation adapts, and the platform’s development priorities respond to what remains.
 All planned In May’s unverified DeepSeek investor meeting transcript, Liang Wenfeng said:
 “So, when it comes to the chip gap between China and the US, I think the software ecosystem gap will eventually disappear. But on the hardware side, we face two separate disadvantages: it takes four Huawei accelerator cards to match one NVIDIA card, and Huawei is also roughly two years behind in bringing its hardware to market.”
 4 months later, the ecosystem gap did indeed narrow. The same transcript mentioned TileLang and helping Huawei get the ecosystem right.
 DSv4.1 Flash Optimizations Another part of the DeepSeek-Huawei symbiosis is that DeepSeek provides Huawei with weights, supporting Day-0 optimized releases, such as DeepSeek V4 and V4.1.
 Ascend’s accumulator design forces a different approach to attention. The Cube’s L0C buffer cannot rescale accumulated outputs in place, while returning a rescaled output to L0C would require an expensive identity-matrix multiplication. DeepSeek instead keeps the running output accumulator in Vector UB , transferring partial sums from L0C when needed for rescaling and accumulation. Hopper holds its accumulator in registers, while Blackwell provides loads and stores between tensor memory and registers, avoiding this particular restriction

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 Profile Huawei also released a profile of one rank of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on a Huawei Ascend 950DT deployment of 32 chips, together with its host threads. In June, we covered a similar profile, that of DeepSeek V4 Pro’s. 

 Many components are similar, like the use of AICPU and separation of some layers to different streams.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 The execution order is 40 target-model layers, the target LM head, 3 DSpark drafter blocks, the draft LM head, and 5 sampling rounds. The main compute runs on Stream 19; the drafter’s run on Stream 173. The V2 MC² kernels that fused computation and communication from the DSv4 Pro trace shows up again, as V3 this time. This is why only 4 AI CPU-launched HCCL operations appear per step, against 43 expert dispatches. These are the target and draft vocabulary heads’ hcom_allGather and hcom_alltoallv : gather hidden states, run the LM-head GEMM, then exchange logits.
 The drafter blocks run once to produce base logits for the draft positions. The subsequent Markov head models token dependencies through sampling and embedding feedback. It does not rerun the transformer blocks for each proposal. The end of each step changes from MoE and attention to a serial chain of small projections and sampling operations.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 As mentioned and explained in previous articles, speculative decoding is a lossless method to predict draft tokens and use a single pass to verify them, amortizing weight loading. In the decode step diagram above, we can see how much faster DSpark token drafting is compared to the verification step.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 DSv4.1 Flash is also the first DeepSeek model to use Engram, but after Qwen and Meituan Longcat . 

 Because Engram takes token IDs as input, the fetch can be done async and overlapped with layer 0’s compute. This allows offloading to DRAM without performance loss vis-a-vis HBM, but offloading to a PCIe 4.0 SSD degrades performance. Read more in our Engram analysis:

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 Summarizing kernel durations in the steady-state window, Stream 19 is occupied for 88.8% of the window but contributes 72.6% of summed device time because other streams overlap it. In the middle, the substantial MIX_AIV and AI_VECTOR_CORE bands contain dispatch/combine as well as quantization.
 Ascend exposes separately scheduled cube and vector paths through MIX_AIC , MIX_AIV , AI_CORE , and AI_VECTOR_CORE . Each event has a task type, so the duration accounting is a partition. Mixed types still involve work beyond a single physical unit; their names do not turn elapsed kernel duration into measured cube-only or vector-only utilization.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 A first-order scenario doubling cube throughput while leaving other device work unchanged gives a 1.32× step improvement. It holds measured stream overlap constant and leaves idle unchanged. This is a composition scenario, not a prediction for new silicon: mixed task types are not exclusive utilization measurements, and bandwidth, dependencies, and scheduling can change the result.
 Quantization fusion likewise remains an opportunity, its attraction is the repeated producer-to-consumer boundary and its large share of the vector bucket that also carries fused communication.
 Ecosystem gaps One issue however is the partnership could work extremely well for DeepSeek without making Ascend equally usable for everyone else. 
 For DeepSeek, building compilers, maintaining kernels and debugging vendor-specific behavior competes with model research and product development, albeit temporarily.
 For everyone else, there may be issues when hardware configurations doesn’t align with DeepSeek’s. Most optimizations were on supernodes, and as of vLLM-Ascend_0.26.0rc1 many issues exist working with Ascend on x86 hosts:
 No DeepGEMM support on x86 hosts
 Dependency on memfabric_hybrid containing hardcoded ARM headers for vLLM-Ascend, blocking startup; vLLM-Ascend doesn’t work out of the box.
 CPU-binding skipped for non-ARM CPUs on vLLM-Ascend
 No NPU + x86 CI, patches needed for some recipes

items.title: Datacenters 2027: The Year of Acceleration, +50GW in a Single Year
items.content:
Not a week goes without another piece of datacenter FUD. We’ve already debunked in depth why moratoriums aren’t as impactful as one may think . Despite that, many still misunderstand the pace of the global AI datacenter buildout. Just the other week, Brad Gerstner from Altimeter showed our data on the All-In Podcast and stated that “SemiAnalysis’ forecast of +43GW in 2027 is too aggressive” and that he thought only about 25GW would get built, close to half of our number, based on his “hunch”. But let’s not operate on hunches.
 It’s very tempting to cede to the FUD given all the constraints on the datacenter buildout: power, labor, supply chains, capital, and many more. But at SemiAnalysis, we care about the truth, not about narratives. And here’s the truth for you: one picture, >24GW of datacenters in advanced stage of construction, most of it to be delivered in 2027. Most of them are more than halfway done, with exterior cooling and electrical equipment already installed. That’s just 40 campuses, a tiny share of the multiple hundred sites in advanced stage of construction. We track them all, and for the full granularity, use our Datacenter Industry Model .

 Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model 
 Of course, there are plenty of challenges and shortages. Behind these pictures, there are labor issues, supply chain delays, fundraising challenges, among many others. We’ve written in-depth about Modular Datacenters and Labor , Datacenter Electrical systems, Cooling systems, Behind-The-Meter power , the US Grid Constraints , and Nvidia’s ecosystem financial support . But the fact is simple: gigantic sites are simply getting built, and many are on time. For example, just go look at what Crusoe built in Abilene, what AWS built in Indiana, or QTS/Microsoft’s giant site in Georgia. These are the sites that have produced SOTA technology like GPT-6 and Fable 5.5. Looking ahead, despite all the constraints, an accelerating number of giant sites keep getting built, as shown by our Top 40 picture

 Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model 
 If you ask any datacenter builder, they’ll tell you how hard it is, how some workers aren’t showing up, how vendors are delayed, and many other issues. All of this is accurate. And that’s why we’ve successfully called out countless datacenter delays and keep calling out developer timelines that appear overly aggressive in our Datacenter model, including the Oracle New Mexico Force Majure site delay in April . To be fair, +50GW is essentially the global cumulative datacenter market up through 2024 being built in one year! But our Datacenter Industry Model adjusts for all of that and still points to a material acceleration in datacenter capacity in 2027. So, what are we seeing that others can’t?

 Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model 
 SemiAnalysis is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support our work, consider becoming a subscriber.

 Let’s dig in. We’ll explore the following topics in this report:
 SemiAnalysis proprietary leading indicators: we’ll show a sneak peak of our proprietary data supporting our forecast, such as self-build construction starts and datacenter leasing (in MWs and USD). Year-to-date, slightly under USD 1T of binding / non-cancellable datacenter leases have been signed – that’s key to supporting our aggressive 2027-28 forecast.
 The shape of the buildout: how can we support +50GW in a single year? Where, what design, what power solutions?
 The “real” question: are we going to face a datacenter oversupply? As we explained in The Great Silicon Shortage , datacenters & power may be the tip of the iceberg, with memory and logic possibly becoming the new #1 constraint in 2027-28.
 Overall, we are very excited about 2027. The natural implication of the acceleration will be significantly more compute supply. That means cheaper and smarter AI, faster pace of AI model progress, and likely material revenue acceleration for leading AI labs and other token vendors. That also means unthinkable capex numbers. Reflexively rates will have to shoot up to enable the buildouts from a capital demand perspective. Let’s dive in!
 SemiAnalysis Datacenter Leading Indicators: how we see the buildout before everyone else Today we want to dive into two crucial indicators that give us strong confidence on our 2027 forecast. The first one is quarterly self-build construction starts. To accurately forecast US hyperscalers, we track the exact construction evolution of every single building. And the conclusion is simple: US hyperscalers have never launched more construction of datacenters. Each quarter, we track how many MWs start construction, and that number is going parabolic, driven in particular by two hyperscalers. If you want to know who or track the granularity of our data, subscribe to our Datacenter Industry Model. 

 Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model 
 The second indicator is Datacenter Leasing. We’ve talked about this a lot in prior reports, but as a quick recap: given the capital-intensity of building multi hundred MW datacenters, developers typically only spend 5-10% of project capital without a customer. They need a “pre-lease” to fund and develop the whole project. That’s typically a 15-20 year contract, with a TCV of $30-50B per GW. Check out our HPC Lease Tracker as part of the Datacenter Model to dive into actual contract economics.
 Subscribe now 
 As such, tracking these lease contracts is a key leading indicator, as it leads debt raises, which itself leads the actual buildout. A big reason why 2026 datacenter growth isn’t “that” high relative to 2025, is that quarterly datacenter leasing remained relatively stable between H2 2023 and H1 2025. Of course, the key reason was the Microsoft Datacenter Freeze, which we called out before anyone else in December 2024 for Datacenter model subscribers : the Redmond giant single-handedly drove the leasing market in 2023 and 2024, then paused, and others could only pick up what was left behind.
 Since H2 2025, things have dramatically changed. Oracle kicked off the era of gigantic leases, after closing on ~4.5GW of datacenter IT capacity across three sites between August and October 2025. Everyone else followed, and the pool of buyers has never been broader, with Meta, AWS, Microsoft, Google, Nvidia, AMD, Anthropic and OpenAI all being in the market for GW-scale leases. There’s also a long tail of Neoclouds signing hundred-MW-scale deals.
 In USD terms, this means an unprecedented amount of lease value that builders can use to raise debt. Just in 2026 year-to-date, we’ve identified over a trillion USD of lease value that was signed and closed . That trillion is supporting a gigantic datacenter buildout in 2027-28. Our new Compute, Capital & Markets Model is now tracking all the debt raises and can confirm that most of this debt has been raised.

 Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model 
 The shape of the buildout: how to build 50GW in a year Tracking all of these leading indicators has enabled us to forecast, before anyone else, the upcoming surge in orders for many industrial suppliers like Vertiv, ABB, Sterling Infrastructure. Check out our Industrials Model for in-depth coverage . However, the challenge is now going from orders to delivery. And resources have obviously become constrained, as power, labor, and sheer regulatory overhead are enormous burdens for developers. But the industry has promptly reacted with innovation.
 The first step is to simplify datacenter designs. We show below how Google has modularized their electrical architecture, removing a significant amount of outdoors cabling that requires onsite assembly, replacing them with prefabricated electrical modules. We track all the equipment changes (including suppliers) for datacenter designs and forecast orders in our Industrials Model 

 Source: SemiAnalysis Industrials Model 
 Others have opted for more radical design changes. One example is Meta with its tent design, that we exclusively unveiled over a year ago . Another one is AWS which has materially simplified their shell design and launched a new rapid design dubbed “SAMDC”. Data halls are also increasingly prefabricated, an effort called Project Houdini at AWS. Construction timelines are now under 10 months. Hence our “ LEGO Datacenters ” title for the modular movement, you literally slot them in and go, and doing so allows for MEP labor (7-11 months of work) to drop up to 63%! We will have a full deep dive on the labor of the 2027 buildout coming soon.

 Source: SemiAnalysis Industrials Model 
 In addition to hyperscale selfbuild, datacenter developers promoting prefabricated designs have also been remarkably successful. DayOne is likely the best example. With a total of ~3GW leased since their first deal in early 2023, the Singaporean company has been a rocket ship in terms of construction speed. While traditional developers have >18 months build timelines, DayOne cut this to ~9 months, which was key to signing huge deals with Firmus, OpenAI and Nvidia.

 Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model 
 Subscribe now 
 Another core issue is power, and again we think the issue is largely solved. We’ve been the first to talk about all issues on power, since March 2024 and subsequently given the grid headroom dips negative at the end of 2027 . This ended up driving AI Labs and hyperscalers to build their own power plants , better known as Behind-the-meter generation, bypassing 5-10year grid interconnection timelines. And while turbine incumbents like GEV quickly faced production bottlenecks, the industry quickly reacted and we’ve since seen a surge in new OEMs and new solutions supplying the market. From fuel cells to truck engines to refurbished turbines, the power generation problem has broadly been solved.

 Source: SemiAnalysis Energy Model 
 In addition, the buildout is now geographically diversifying. This naturally bypasses US labor, power, and (in some countries) permitting constraints. And as shown below, the ex-US buildout is sharply accelerating in 2027, and we expect it to gain a lot of market share in 2028, largely driven by US challenges.

 Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model 
 The Real Question: Will We Have an Oversupply of Datacenters?

items.title: ASML Is Building a Hybrid Bonding Tool!
items.content:
ASML has not announced anything yet, but its patent filings, a news report and its own roadmap all suggest so. We believe it will start with a die-to-wafer (D2W) hybrid bonding (HB) tool. This is harder to build than wafer-to-wafer but is where ASML could gain an edge. We see the move as a natural extension of ASML’s vertical integration, and one that should strengthen its customer ties.
 In this article we unpack the tool’s design end to end, starting with patent filings. What makes it unique is that it runs on a track . That changes how the tool and the dies move: each die rides its own holder past the process stations, and the tools get closer at each station to process the dies. The track’s independent shuttles also lift station utilization, save on duplicate tooling, and enable heterogeneous integration.
 We believe ASML could gain an edge in alignment accuracy and particle control for Hybrid Bonding. These are the two factors that set bonding yield. And ASML has expertise in solving the same problems in lithography.
 Despite the advantages, ASML still needs to solve challenges around feed-forward metrology, the die-to-wafer contact, the modification of the non-bonding tools so they can process dies on the track, and keeping the whole loop clean.
 We expect advanced logic, where D2W already runs in volume, to adopt ASML’s D2W HB tool first. This is bad news for Besi . Logic accounts for most of Besi’s HB business today concentrated at TSMC and Intel. ASML has been working with both for more than two decades and just announced a joint photomask initiative in September. We won’t be surprised to see a similar move in the back end process. Besi’s HBM prospects are also weakening. Korean challengers are catching up, in addition to an HBM adoption that we expect to slip to 2029 or beyond.
 ASML is Building a Hybrid Bonder We did a deep dive on hybrid bonding in 2024, and we still see it as the most transformative innovation in semiconductor manufacturing since EUV. Wafer-to-wafer (W2W) hybrid bonding (HB) is already in volume in image sensors and 3D NAND, and DRAM makers will be next. Die-to-wafer (D2W) HB is moving slower , because the industry still lacks mature tools that combine satisfying alignment accuracy and throughput (our check indicates upper bound in current applications is only one wafer per hour), which keeps cost per die high. Today D2W runs in volume only in logic: AMD has shipped hybrid-bonded V-Cache since 2022, and TSMC’s SoIC bonds at about 6um pitch today and targets 4.5um around 2029. The market expected HBM to become the big D2W volume driver from 2028. However, our view is different: we believe HBM will not adopt D2W HB before 2029 , if at all.
 Besi has led D2W and is the only supplier with tools in volume production. Everyone else is still trying to get a first tool qualified. But we believe the situation will soon change, because ASML is building a D2W hybrid bonding tool. Management hasn’t announced anything yet. But the company filed 27 bonding patent families between December 2022 and November 2024, most of them D2W, and the true count is likely higher because filings made after November 2024 are not yet public. The Elec also reported in March that ASML had started the architecture design of a hybrid bonder with Prodrive Technologies and VDL ETG.
 In the anchor filing ( WO2025201788A1 ), ASML drew how its bonding flow works. Interestingly, the system looks nothing like a traditional D2W bonder (see Advanced Packaging Part 5 for how those work). Instead of a bond head picking each die off a diced wafer and placing it, ASML moves single dies on independent holders around a track (Fig 1). Each die passes inspection, cleaning, plasma activation and metrology (topography, leveling and alignment) stations before it reaches the bonding station where the chuck lifts the bottom wafer up to meet the die. We unpack the design in the sections below.
 Fig 1: ASML’s track-based D2W bonder, SA annotated and simplified 

 Source: ASML; SemiAnalysis Wafer Fabrication Equipment Model 
 ASML could be building a W2W hybrid bonding tool as well. According to a patent analysis by Inha University , ASML is likely building W2W HB equipment on its TWINSCAN platform, leaning on its wafer overlay accuracy. We focus on the D2W machine in this note, because it is the harder tool to build and the one where ASML could gain a real edge.
 …as Part of its Vertical Integration Initiative We believe this is a continuation of ASML’s effort to integrate vertically and tighten customer relationships. ASML bought Cymer for its light source in 2013, HMI for e-beam inspection in 2016 and Berliner Glas for optics modules in 2020. It shipped its first back-end product, the XT:260 i-line packaging scanner, in 3Q25. And most recently, ASML announced joint initiatives with TSMC , Intel Foundry and Samsung to move the industry from 6-inch to 12-inch photomasks for High NA EUV.
 Building a bonder would be a natural next step. In fact, ASML’s own roadmap already puts bonding inside the front-end flow. Its 2024 Investor Day listed W2W and D2W hybrid bonding for NAND, DRAM and logic (Fig 2). And a July 2024 filing shows how the bonder and the scanner would work together by sharing die position data. Today a scanner printing on a bonded wafer must pre-align and coarse-align every die before it can expose. In ASML’s design the bonder already knows where it put each die and hands that map (a “coordinate system” in the filing) to the scanner, which checks a few marks and exposes. Customers get faster lithography on bonded wafers, and ASML gets to sell the bonder and the scanner as a pair.
 Fig 2: ASML’s map of front-end 3D integration 

 Source: ASML Investor Day, 14-Nov-2024 
 We expect advanced logic to be the first adopter. Logic is where D2W HB already runs in volume, and where the alignment requirement keeps tightening. TSMC calls overlay “always the biggest challenge” for SoIC. As its HB pitch moves from 6um to 4.5um by 2029, the placement accuracy requirement will tighten further. ASML is strong in alignment, as we will elaborate below, so an edge here should help it win logic customers first. Advanced logic dies are also among the most expensive chips, so logic customers can afford a premium tool. We expect ASML to price its tools at a premium to peers.
 In the next three sections, we discuss (1) the tool’s track system - the most unusual thing about it compared with what is on the market; (2) how ASML’s strengths in alignment, particle control and motion could make its HB tool superior; and (3) the challenges ASML or its supply chain partners still need to resolve to build a working tool. Let’s dive in.
 What’s Unique About the Tool One of the most interesting things about the tool is that it runs on a track . ASML names SuperTrak CONVEYANCE (Fig 3) as an example in its patent filing , so we assume it uses that track and we base our analysis on the track’s published design.
 The fundamental difference from a traditional bonder is where the die lives. In a Besi-type tool, the die is prepared elsewhere, and a bond head picks it up only for the final placement. In ASML’s design, each die sits on its own holder from the moment it leaves the carrier and stays there until the bonding step . The process stations are built around the track: the die stops in front of a station, the station cleans, activates or measures it in place, and the die moves on.
 Fig 3: SuperTrak CONVEYANCE track (HORIZON10 platform) 

 Source: Company website 
 Now let’s go through the process step by step . For illustration, we took the patent drawing and labelled every station in Fig 4. A gripper takes the die off its carrier and sets it on an empty substrate holder (206), which carries it along the track (202). The die stops in turn at the inspection, cleaning, plasma activation, topographic inspection, leveling, coarse alignment, position adjustment and fine alignment stations (210 to 226). At each stop the die stays on its holder, and the station does its work. Note the reversal here: in the patent it is the station’s sensor or head that moves in to reach the die, not the die that is carried into the tool as in today’s flow. After these steps the die arrives at the bonding station (228).
 This bonding station deserves a closer look . The first thing to note is that the final placement is done by the holder (206) and the chuck (234), not the track: SuperTrak’s spec sheet puts the shuttles’ repeatability at about 10um, nowhere near the 50nm placement accuracy the bond needs. Next, zoom in on the right-hand part of Fig 4 for the bonding work. The chuck lifts the bottom wafer to within tens of microns of the die, the holder’s actuators adjust the die’s position, the die is pressed onto the wafer to form the bond, and the holder releases it. The empty holder then starts another loop.
 Fig 4: Patent WO2025201788A1 Fig. 2 (left) and Fig. 6 side view (right), SA annotated 

 Source: ASML; SemiAnalysis Wafer Fabrication Equipment Model 
 This design has three major benefits:
 First, independent shuttles lift the utilization of every station . The number of stations per step can be set from that step’s cycle time: a three-second cleaning step gets three stations, and a 1.2-second bond step gets one, so every station stays busy. The patent asks for exactly this, to “occupy all process stations simultaneously”.
 Second, capacity is added by adding a station rather than a second tool, as long as the equipment chamber has room for it. That saves duplicate tooling and budget .
 Last but not least, the design suits heterogeneous integration : a new die type is a new software recipe, so mixed chiplets could share one line.
 That said, the track brings its own challenges around the non-bonding stations and the cleanliness of the whole loop. We come back to them later.
 How ASML May Gain an Edge Before that, let’s look at how ASML could bring its existing strengths to the HB tool.
 First, a reminder of why alignment accuracy and cleanliness matter so much in hybrid bonding. As we elaborated before , a single 1um particle between two full-thickness wafers can unbond an area around 10mm across , resulting in a defective bond (Fig 5). So particle control is extremely important for HB. Alignment matters for two reasons: placement accuracy sets bond yield directly, and alignment time weighs far more on D2W throughput than on W2W because it compounds with the die count. These two hurdles are what make hybrid bonding almost a front-end process.
 Fig 5: A small particle opens a void and an open contact in hybrid bonding 

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 We believe ASML can tackle both with decades of experience solving the same two problems in lithography.
 For alignment, we believe ASML can reuse its wafer-alignment sensor technology. Based on its patent filings , the bonding system puts a tiny diffraction grating on each die and reads the die’s position from the light the grating scatters. The principle is the same as ORION , the wafer-alignment sensor on every new TWINSCAN since 2017. ORION was built to read marks that CMP and etch have tilted or deformed (Fig 6), and a mark on a bonding die goes through the same CMP and plasma activation as the copper pads next to it, so it carries the same asymmetry. We believe the same sensor family can serve the D2W bonder.
 Fig 6: A symmetric and a tilted alignment mark. Process steps shift the apparent center; ORION’s multi-color readout was built to see through that 

 Source: ASML, Aligning lithography to the nanometer, Dec-2021 
 Its sensing and motion capabilities also provide it with more room in total alignment error budget. Its NXT:2100i holds 0.9nm overlay on a single machine. And ASML can already measure the distortion of a W2W bonded wafer and correct the next lithography layer for it, bringing post-bond overlay from 40-60nm down to below 4nm (Fig 7). These are litho numbers, not bond results. But they mean ASML’s sensor and stage errors sit more than an order of magnitude below the 50nm a bonder needs. Higher stage precision leaves more room in a bonder’s error budget for the other factors: die shift on the holder, thermal drift and movement during contact.
 Fig 7: ASML metrology plus scanner correction brings post-bond overlay to 2.5-3.9nm 

 Source: ASML Investor Day, 14-Nov-2024 
 Prodrive Technologies and VDL ETG are the likely component suppliers to help ASML’s bonder move fast on motion. Prodrive makes the linear motors and drives for ASML’s EUV maglev stages and has also built Hanwha Semitech’s SHB2 Nano bonder. VDL ETG builds ASML’s frames and modules (Fig 8).
 Fig 8: Prodrive’s linear motor (left) and VDL ETG’s wafer handler module (right) 

 Source: Company websites 
 On cleanliness, the requirements for ASML’s EUV systems are more strict as a bonder’s. Few tool makers have fought particles at the nanometer scale for as long as ASML. EUV scanners move reticles and wafers in vacuum and keep reticle particle adders at a level “ compatible with HVM requirements for sub-10nm node lithography ”. We believe ASML has thought about the bonding surfaces too: its bonding apparatus filing adds a tool that cleans the substrate supports and a sensor that watches their flatness, particle load and distortion.
 That said, contaminants in a bonder differ from those in a scanner. Most are dicing debris on die edges and particles landing on freshly activated, hydrophilic surfaces. We look for more detail on how ASML handles these bonder-specific contaminants in future filings.
 After the paywall we discuss the challenges ASML needs to tackle to build a working tool, and how its tool will impact on Besi’s business prospects.
 Open Questions ASML Needs to Solve
